summary.text: Nitrous oxide, N₂O, is an oxide of nitrogen known as laughing gas, a colourless, non-flammable gas with a slightly sweet scent at room temperature.
It is the third most important greenhouse gas, adding substantially to global warming, and a major scavenger of stratospheric ozone, comparable to CFCs.
About 40% of human-caused emissions come from farming, where soil micro-organisms digest nitrogen fertilisers into the gas.

items.prompt: A farmer spreads nitrogen fertiliser across a field. How does that end up adding nitrous oxide to the air?

options.label: Sunlight splits the fertiliser into gas
Soil microbes digest it into the gas
The growing crops breathe the gas out
Rain reacts with it to release the gas

items.explain: About 40% of human-caused emissions come from agriculture, as soil micro-organisms digest nitrogen fertilisers into nitrous oxide.

items.prompt: Why did nitrous oxide come to be nicknamed laughing gas?

options.label: Breathing it in can bring on euphoria
It hisses from its tank like a chuckle
It was first made as a party joke
It tickles the throat and makes people cough

items.explain: Humphry Davy coined the name to describe the euphoric effects of inhaling it; some users get the giggles and burst into laughter.

items.prompt: A nervous patient at the dentist breathes nitrous oxide while also getting a numbing injection. What job does the gas do here?

options.label: It numbs the tooth fully on its own
It knocks the patient out for hours
It disinfects the mouth before work
It eases anxiety alongside the injection

items.explain: Today nitrous oxide is used in dentistry to reduce anxiety, as an add-on to local anaesthetic rather than a replacement for it.

items.prompt: Besides warming the planet, what other harm does nitrous oxide do high in the atmosphere?

options.label: It forms thick clouds that block sunlight
It turns rain into strong acid
It destroys stratospheric ozone
It cools the upper air and stirs storms

items.explain: Nitrous oxide is a major scavenger of stratospheric ozone, with an impact comparable to CFCs, as well as a greenhouse gas.

items.prompt: Hospitals of the 1840s chose diethyl ether over nitrous oxide for major surgery. Why?

options.label: Nitrous oxide was too flammable to use
Nitrous oxide was too weak an anaesthetic
Nitrous oxide had been banned by law
Nitrous oxide was far too costly to make

items.explain: Nitrous oxide was not found strong enough for major surgery, so the stronger, more potent ether was accepted instead in 1846.

items.prompt: In 1844 dentist Horace Wells reported good results with nitrous oxide, yet other dentists did not take it up. What most likely held them back?

options.label: The gas was not yet possible to produce
Patients refused to breathe any gas
Ether had already replaced it everywhere
His public demonstration in Boston partly failed

items.explain: Wells's first public demonstration in Boston in January 1845 was partly unsuccessful, leaving colleagues doubtful about its efficacy and safety.

paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: Nitrous oxide is a compound of nitrogen and oxygen with the formula N₂O. Its common names include laughing gas and simply nitrous. At room temperature it is a colourless gas that does not burn and has a slightly sweet smell and taste. When hot, though, it becomes a strong oxidiser, behaving much like oxygen itself.

paragraphs.heading: Its part in climate change
paragraphs.text: Nitrous oxide also pollutes the atmosphere. In 2026 the air held 340 parts per billion (ppb) of it, and the level rises by about 1 ppb each year. It ranks as the third most important greenhouse gas and adds substantially to global warming. It also destroys a great deal of the ozone in the stratosphere, with an effect on the scale of CFCs. Cutting emissions is an important aim of climate politics.

paragraphs.heading: Farms and fertiliser
paragraphs.text: Roughly 40% of the nitrous oxide that people cause comes from farming. When nitrogen fertilisers go onto fields, micro-organisms in the soil digest them and turn them into the gas.

paragraphs.heading: Uses in medicine and beyond
paragraphs.text: The gas has important medical uses, above all in surgery and dentistry, because it numbs pain and works as an anaesthetic. The World Health Organization includes it on its List of Essential Medicines. In dentistry today it is used to calm anxiety alongside a local anaesthetic. Outside medicine, it serves as an oxidiser in rocket propellants and racing fuels, and as the gas that froths whipped cream.

paragraphs.heading: Why it is called laughing gas
paragraphs.text: Humphry Davy coined the name laughing gas, after the euphoria people feel when they breathe it in. Users often seem dreamy and sedated, but some get the giggles and burst out laughing. That brief high makes it attractive as a recreational drug, and laughing gas parties caught on at once in 1799. Used heavily over time, it can damage the nerves by switching off vitamin B₁₂.

paragraphs.heading: From discovery to the dentist
paragraphs.text: Joseph Priestley first made the gas in 1772. Davy later found that breathing it could relieve a conscious person's pain, and suggested it could be used in surgery. Even so, 44 more years passed before doctors tried it for anaesthesia. On 11 December 1844 the dentist Horace Wells used it to pull a tooth without pain. It came into general use only from 1863, when Gardner Quincy Colton began using it in his dental clinics, and in the next three years his team gave it to over 25,000 patients.
